# ADR-008: UUIDv7, generated by the application

Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-09-29

## Context

Every public identifier in this API is a UUID, and the schema is shared by two
backends. Two questions had to be answered together: which UUID version, and
which side generates it.

The version matters because of index locality. UUIDv4 is random across its whole
range, so consecutive inserts land in unrelated leaf pages of the primary key's
B-tree. As a table grows past memory, that turns one sequential write into many
scattered ones and the index fragments. UUIDv7 puts a millisecond timestamp in
the high bits, so newly generated values sort near each other and inserts append
to the right-hand edge of the index the way a bigserial would.

Who generates it matters because of `stock_reservations` and checkout. Checkout
locks variant rows in ascending UUID order to avoid deadlocking two baskets that
share items in opposite orders. That ordering has to be identical in TypeScript,
in Java, and in PostgreSQL's `ORDER BY`, or the cross-backend concurrency test
fails against whichever implementation sorts differently.

## Decision

The applications generate **UUIDv7** identifiers themselves. Columns keep
`DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` as a fallback so that seed data, fixtures, and manual
`INSERT`s work without either application running.

Ordering is defined on the **canonical lowercase hyphenated string form**, which
is also what the API emits. For UUIDs in this form, lexicographic string
comparison, byte-wise comparison, and PostgreSQL's `uuid` comparison all produce
the same order — hex digits ascend in ASCII and the hyphens sit at fixed
positions. So `[...ids].sort()` in TypeScript, `Collections.sort` on
`List<String>` in Java, and `ORDER BY id` in SQL agree, and the lock ordering
rule can be stated once for all three.

## Alternatives considered

- **`gen_random_uuid()` in the database, as the only source.** Simplest — no
  library on either side, nothing to keep in sync. Rejected because it makes
  every identifier unknowable until after the `INSERT` returns, which forces an
  extra round trip wherever the application needs the id before writing related
  rows, and because UUIDv4's index behaviour is the thing we are trying to
  avoid. Kept as a column default, just not as the primary mechanism.
- **`bigserial` primary keys with a separate public UUID.** Best index behaviour
  of all the options, and a real pattern. Rejected as two identifiers per row
  for a 15-product demo: double the columns, double the joins to reason about,
  and a permanent question of which one any given piece of code means.
- **UUIDv7 generated by PostgreSQL.** Postgres 18 ships `uuidv7()`, which would
  put generation back in one place. Rejected because this project targets
  PostgreSQL 16, and because it reintroduces the round-trip problem above.
- **ULID.** Same time-ordering benefit, shorter textual form. Rejected because it
  is not a UUID: it would need a custom column type or a `varchar`, giving up
  PostgreSQL's native `uuid` comparison and validation, and every client library
  would need a converter.
- **Ordering locks on the raw 16 bytes rather than the string.** Equivalent
  result, but it obliges each implementation to get its own byte-extraction
  right — `UUID.getMostSignificantBits()` in Java is signed, which is exactly
  the kind of detail that produces a sort order that is correct in one language
  and subtly wrong in the other. Comparing the canonical string is harder to get
  wrong and is what the API already exposes.

## Consequences

- Both implementations need a UUIDv7 generator: `uuid` v10+ (`uuidv7()`) on the
  Node side, `com.fasterxml.uuid` or an equivalent on the Java side. They must
  agree on the version, not on the exact library.
- Identifiers leak their creation time to anyone holding one. Acceptable here —
  order numbers and product slugs are already sequential or public — but it
  would not be acceptable for something like a password reset token, which is
  why those use random bytes instead.
- A row inserted by the seed or by hand gets a v4 identifier from the column
  default, so the table will contain a mix of versions. Nothing depends on the
  version of any particular id, only on the ordering being total and consistent,
  which holds across versions.
- The lock ordering rule is now testable in isolation: sort the same list of ids
  in both languages and in SQL, and assert all three match. That test belongs
  with the checkout unit tests in task 2.8 and its Java port in 5.3.

## Register

This ADR is not in the original register in the
[Reference Hub](https://app.clickup.com/t/z8v9xnfz54), which runs 001–007. It was
written during task 1.3, whose checklist calls for the UUID decision to be
recorded as an ADR. The register on the board needs a row for it.
